title: The filioque
hook: Western churches added and the Son to the creed about the Spirit; the Orthodox did not, and the argument continues gently

segments.voice: Yesterday, pictures of the Trinity: the sun, a lover and love, a shamrock. Your line was every picture falls short. When did your words stop fitting someone you love? Day one thousand seventy-one.

Sunday morning, two churches on the same street. In one, the people stand and say the Nicene Creed, and when they reach the Holy Spirit they say: who proceeds from the Father and the Son. Across the street, in an Orthodox church, the people say the same creed, and at the same spot they say: who proceeds from the Father. Then both go on. Same creed. Same Spirit. A difference of a few words in English, and in Latin, just one. That one word has a long story. Today's word: filioque.

Filioque is Latin for and the Son. The Nicene Creed, as the early councils agreed it in Greek, said the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father. That echoes Jesus at the Last Supper in John's Gospel: "the Spirit of truth, which proceedeth from the Father." In the West, where the church prayed in Latin, churches came to add one word, filioque, so the line said the Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son. The English prayer book carries it: "Who proceedeth from the Father and the Son." Catholic and Anglican churches, among others in the West, have said it that way. Orthodox Christians say the creed without it. They hold two things. First, a creed agreed by the whole church shouldn't be changed by one part of it. Second, they speak of the Father as the one source within the Trinity. Western teachers answer that the word guards the bond between the Son and the Spirit. And they point to the very same verse, where Jesus says of the Spirit, "whom I will send unto you from the Father." Notice that sentence holds both: the Son sends; the Spirit proceeds from the Father. Orthodox teachers reply that sending in time is not the same as proceeding in eternity. Each side leans on a different half. This one word became one of the disagreements in the long, painful parting between East and West. It's still not settled. But in recent times the tone has grown gentler, with Catholic and Orthodox leaders talking it through patiently, and some Western churches leaving the word out when they pray alongside the Orthodox. One word, and a long argument held more and more carefully.

Here's the practice: say the creed's line both ways. Settle, and breathe. Quietly, say the Western form: I believe in the Holy Ghost, the Lord and giver of life, who proceedeth from the Father and the Son. Breathe. Now say the Eastern form: I believe in the Holy Ghost, the Lord and giver of life, who proceedeth from the Father. Breathe. Say each once more, slowly. Notice what changes, and how much stays the same. Then hold in mind the people who will say each one this Sunday, on their own streets. If you pray, you can pray for both. The bell holds the time.
Filioque. Latin for and the Son: one word Western churches say in the creed and the Orthodox do not.

Your line: one word, long argument. This week walked through the book and its depths: how the Bible was gathered, God-breathed, four senses, not-knowing, almighty, pictures of the Trinity, and one small word. Today, in any old disagreement of your own, try a gentler tone. Day one thousand seventy-one.

howItsDone: Catholic, Anglican and other Western churches say in the Nicene Creed that the Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son; Orthodox churches say from the Father, keeping the creed's older wording.

fork.setup: you're at the Last Supper, and Jesus is speaking about the Spirit of truth who is coming. where does he say the Spirit proceeds from?
fork.reveal: "the Spirit of truth, which proceedeth from the Father." in the same verse he says he will send the Spirit from the Father. Western readers lean on the sending; Orthodox readers say sending in time is not proceeding in eternity.

trapdoor: what you thought: a technical word nobody needs.
what it means: one Latin word in the creed, and the Son, said in Western churches and not by the Orthodox.
what a scholar hears: John 15:26 holds both halves in one verse: the Son sends the Spirit, and the Spirit proceeds from the Father.

notes: Week end (day 1071 = 7 × 153): the carry looks back over days 1065–1071.
Claims rule: no dates given (Constantinople 381, Toledo 589, Rome 1014, 1054). 'The long, painful parting between East and West' and 'one of the disagreements' are kept general. Confirm.

'In recent times the tone has grown gentler ... some Western churches leaving the word out when they pray alongside the Orthodox' is a general claim about recent ecumenical practice (e.g. popes reciting the creed without the filioque with the Ecumenical Patriarch; Eastern Catholic use; some Anglican provinces). Confirm or soften.

The practice's two forms ('the Lord and giver of life, who proceedeth from the Father ...') are spoken without quotation marks; only 'Who proceedeth from the Father and the Son' is quoted from the BCP 1662 creed. Check wording against the 1662 text.

Orthodox position summarized as: a creed of the whole church shouldn't be altered by one part, and the Father as the one source (monarchy of the Father). Western: the phrase guards the Son–Spirit bond. Check fairness for both.

Audit: teach and fork reveal gave the Western reading of John 15:26 without the Orthodox reply; added the standard Orthodox distinction (the Son's sending of the Spirit in time vs the Spirit's eternal procession from the Father) so neither side is left unanswered.

Editor pass: garbled practice line ('sit with the people who say each one, on their streets') rewritten; 'say it that way' softened to 'have said it that way', since some Anglican churches now leave the word out.
